newsitem.title: HUNGARY: 1996 was a good year for Hungarian exporters.
newsitem.headline: 1996 was a good year for Hungarian exporters.

text.p: Hungary's export-led companies will take top honours for 1996 earnings figures but analysts say rising domestic consumption this year will help companies more exposed to the domestic market.
"Overall, 1996 was the year of the exporters and 1997 should be the year of those who can exploit the domestic economy," said James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London.
Another London-based analyst voice a similar opinion as Hungarian bourse-listed companies prepared to publish their preliminary annual results by February 15.
"We tend to favour more the export-orientated companies rather than the domestic demand companies, at least for 1996," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.

"Domestic demand has been fairly weak and exports have done relatively well, particularly compared to other countries, not only to western Europe but also, I think more particularly to eastern Europe."

Average real wages of Hungary's industrial, retail and service sectors fell 3.6 percent in the January-November period of 1996 year-on-year, and showed a declining trend from a 7.2 percent fall for the first half of last year, according to the central statistical office's data.

The growth rate in Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to be flat for 1996. The central statistical office's latest figures showed that GDP grew one percent in the third quarter of 1996 from the same period of 1995.
For 1997, Hungary targets an up to three percent GDP growth amid the revival of investments and domestic consumption.
In 1996 the pharmaceuticals are expected to do well, but Oates has other favourites, like quality meat processor Pick and oil company MOL.

"I also think that Pick is possibly slightly under-recognised, given that they are so exposed to exports," Oates said. In Pick's sales exports usually account for more than one-third of its total revenues.
"It seems quite possible that MOL has the potential to surprise on the upside rather than the downside...that's a good reason for the stock to go up," Oates said.
"People now believe that business is improving and they can develop over the next two to three years."

HSBC's Rendell expected the banks to do "reasonably well because of lower provisions" in 1996, and was optimistic on home improvement product maker Graboplast, saying it did well on its export markets, particularly in eastern Europe.
"Any company with an exposure of its export market to eastern Europe should do better than average," he added.
Analysts expected 1997 to bring substantial changes, giving more upside potential for domestic-oriented companies.
"I think in 1997 the conditions will change dramatically and companies that are more exposed to the domestic market ought to do a lot better," UBS's Oates said.
"Looking forward to 1997 we start to switch more to the domestic companies, particularly in the second half of this year," HSBC's Rendell said.

"We think the domestic-orientated companies will do better because interest rates are coming down in Hungary, the domestic economy is picking up," he said. "We are looking forward to quite a strong recovery in GDP this year of about three percent."
An improving domestic economy, however, does not mean that exporters could not boost their performance this year.
"The chemicals probably had an average year for 1996, that is picking up going into 1997, because of cuts in taxes will help them," Rendell said.

Analysts said they were confident that the rally of the Budapest Stock Exchange, which has already risen 30 percent this year, will continue after the release of earnings reports, although not to the same degree.
"I think there are some stocks that will win and some that will lose, but overall I think there could still be some growth come," Oates said.

"There are reasons to be cautiously optimistic about the Hungarian market. I think the pharmaceuticals companies do look expensive but on the other hand I think MOL looks quite cheap," UBS's Oates said.
